a: Her images are put to shame; / her filthy idols are shattered.
t: The line about images and idols
p: The Greek has no line about Babylon's idols; the Hebrew has it.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: Her images are put to shame; / her filthy idols are shattered.

readings.w: Septuagint (Greek 27:2, Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus)

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew: the line fits the parallel of Bel and Marduk, and a copyist is more likely to drop a repeated line than add one.
b: The Greek keeps 'Bel was put to shame' and a second line about Marduk (Maiodak), then goes on to verse 3. The Hebrew line uses a word for idols found often in Ezekiel (gillulim, 'filthy idols'). The Greek Jeremiah is about one-seventh shorter than the Hebrew, and Emanuel Tov and others hold that it translates an earlier, shorter edition of the Hebrew; a minority view is that the Greek translator or a later copyist abridged. This entry does not settle that. Apart from 50:4-6 (see the variant at 50:4), no Qumran copy preserves any verse of chapters 50-52, so none of the entries below cites a scroll unless it says so.

a: In those days and at that time, the LORD declares,
t: 'In those days and at that time' (4QJer-e)
p: The scroll lacks 'in the days' and has 'those' after 'at that time'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: In those days and at that time, the LORD declares,

readings.w: 4QJer-e (4Q72b; Abegg-Bowley-Cook transcription)
readings.plain: And at that time those, the LORD declares,

readings.w: Septuagint (Greek 27:4, Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus)
readings.plain: In those days and at that time, the LORD declares,
readings.orig: ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις ἐκείναις καὶ ἐν τῷ καιρῷ ἐκείνῳ

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew of the Masoretic Text, which the Greek supports. The phrase 'in those days and at that time' is a stock opening in Jeremiah (33:15; 50:20).
b: The scroll is the only Qumran copy of any verse of chapters 50-52. The transcription gives 'and at that time' followed by 'those', marked as different from the Masoretic Text; the words 'in the days' are not there. The difference is small and may be a copyist's correction. Elsewhere in 50:4-6 the scroll agrees with the Masoretic Text apart from spelling (see the note on 50:6).

a: the hope of their ancestors, the LORD
t: Hope of their ancestors, or the one who gathered them?
p: The Hebrew calls the LORD 'hope'. The Greek calls him 'the one who gathered their ancestors'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: the hope of their ancestors, the LORD

readings.w: Septuagint (Greek 27:7, Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus)
readings.plain: the one who gathered their ancestors

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew. 'The hope of Israel' is a title of the LORD in 14:8 and 17:13, so the Hebrew reading has support within the book.
b: The Greek translator may have read the same consonants as a form of 'gather' (qavah), which gives 'the one who gathered' and also changes the grammar of the line. The Hebrew can also be pointed to mean 'pool of water' (miqveh), as in 17:13. The reading is not found in a scroll.

a: From the oppressor's sword
t: The oppressor's sword or the Greek sword?
p: The Hebrew has 'oppressing'. The Greek has 'Greek', as if the word were Yavan (Ionia).

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: From the oppressor's sword

readings.w: Septuagint (Greek 27:16, Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus)
readings.plain: From the Greek sword

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew. The same phrase 'the oppressing sword' is in 46:16. A 'Greek sword' would be odd in a poem about Babylon in the 500s BC.
b: The Greek translator probably took the word as Yavan (Ionia, Greece). That is a Greek reading and not evidence of an older Hebrew.

a: the people of Leb-qamai
t: Leb-qamai or Chaldea?
p: The Hebrew has a cipher word. The Greek has a plain word.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: the people of Leb-qamai

readings.w: Septuagint (Greek 28:1, Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus)
readings.plain: the Chaldeans who live there

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew and explains the cipher in a note. Both explanations of the Greek are possible, and the witnesses do not settle which is right.
b: Leb-qamai spells 'Chaldeans' in the atbash cipher. The Greek has 'Chaldeans'. Two explanations. (1) The Greek translator's Hebrew read Kasdim, and the cipher entered the Hebrew text later. This is the usual argument in the debate about the two editions (see Tov): the Greek also lacks the cipher Sheshach in 25:26 and 51:41, which points to a Hebrew source without the ciphers. (2) The translator recognized the cipher and wrote what it meant. That would explain 51:1, but it does not explain why he left Sheshach out, since a translator who could decode one cipher could have decoded the other. The Plain follows the Hebrew that has come down.

a: I will send outsiders to Babylon
t: Outsiders or insolent men?
p: One letter differs: zarim 'outsiders', or zedim 'insolent men'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: I will send outsiders to Babylon

readings.w: Septuagint (Greek 28:2, Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus)
readings.plain: I will send insolent men to Babylon

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew. Outsiders fits the winnowing and the stripping of the land. The Greek's 'insolent men' probably reads zedim, which looks almost the same (the letters resh and dalet are easily confused).
b: This entry gives two readings that differ in one letter. Neither is preserved in a scroll.

a: The archer must not draw his bow;
t: Let the archer draw, or let him not?
p: The Masoretic Text, the Vulgate and the Targum say 'not'. The Greek says 'let him draw'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008), with a Ketiv/Qere
readings.plain: The archer must not draw his bow;
readings.orig: אל ידרך הדרך קשתו ואל יתעל בסרינו

readings.w: Septuagint (Greek 28:3, Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus)
readings.plain: Let the archer bend his bow;
readings.orig: τεινέτω ὁ τείνων τὸ τόξον αὐτοῦ, καὶ περιθέσθω ᾧ ἐστὶν ὅπλα αὐτοῦ

readings.w: Vulgate and Targum Jonathan
readings.plain: Let the archer not bend his bow;
readings.orig: לָא יִמְתַּח דִמְתַּח קַשְׁתֵּיהּ וְלָא יִסַק בְּסִרְיָנַיָהּ (Targum)

why: The Plain follows the Masoretic Text, which the Vulgate and the Targum share. The Greek's positive command may be a translator's choice for the same consonants (al, 'not', or el), and it also changes the speaker of the line (see the note).
b: The Hebrew consonants al can be read 'not'. The Masoretes also mark a second yidrokh as read but not written. The JPS Tanakh (Gender-Sensitive Edition) reads positively, 'Let the archer draw his bow', and notes that some Hebrew manuscripts and ancient versions read 'Let not'. No Qumran copy preserves this verse.

a: the spirit of the kings of Media
t: Kings or king of Media?
p: The Hebrew has a plural. The Greek has a singular.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: the spirit of the kings of Media

readings.w: Septuagint (Greek 28:11, Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus)
readings.plain: the spirit of the king of Media

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew. The plural is the harder reading, and the singular could be the translator's simplification.
b: The Greek also has the singular in 51:28 ('the king of the Medes'). Both readings fit what is known of the Persian-Median state after Cyrus.

a: How Sheshach has been taken, / the pride of all the earth caught!
t: Sheshach is missing from the Greek
p: The cipher name Sheshach is in the Hebrew and not in the Greek.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: How Sheshach has been taken, / the pride of all the earth caught!
readings.orig: אֵיךְ נִלְכְּדָה שֵׁשַׁךְ וַתִּתָּפֵשׂ תְּהִלַּת כָּל הָאָרֶץ

readings.w: Septuagint (Greek 28:41, Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus)
readings.plain: How the pride of all the earth has been taken and caught!
readings.orig: πῶς ἑάλω καὶ ἐθηρεύθη τὸ καύχημα πάσης τῆς γῆς

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew. The cipher is hard to explain as an addition by a copyist who did not know it, but the Greek has the plain 'Chaldeans' for the other cipher (51:1), so the two ciphers are not treated alike.
b: Sheshach is also missing in the Greek at the end of Hebrew 25:26 (Greek 32:12). Either the earlier Hebrew had no cipher (the argument for this is stated at 51:1), or the translator dropped what he did not understand. Rashi says Sheshach is Babylon in the atbash cipher.

a: I will call Bel to account in Babylon;
t: Bel in Babylon, or just Babylon?
p: The Greek has no mention of Bel.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: I will call Bel to account in Babylon;

readings.w: Septuagint (Greek 28:44, Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus)
readings.plain: I will call Babylon to account;

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew; the lines about what Bel swallowed need his name.
b: The Greek goes on to say 'I will bring out what he swallowed from her mouth', making Babylon the swallower. It ends the verse with 'the nations will no more be gathered to her'. The rest of the Hebrew text through 51:49a is lacking in the Greek (see the next entries).

a: Even the wall of Babylon has fallen.
t: The fallen wall
p: The last line of verse 44 is not in the Greek.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: Even the wall of Babylon has fallen.

readings.w: Septuagint (Greek 28:44, Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus)

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew. The Greek omits 51:44b-49a as one block, which fits an earlier, shorter text or a copying skip. No other witness decides.
b: This entry goes with the next five (51:45-49). Together they are about 110 words. Verse 45 echoes 51:6, 'save your life'.

a: Come out of her, my people! / Let each one save his life / from the LORD's blazing anger.

p: The Greek has no 51:45.

readings.w: Septuagint (Greek 28:45, Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus)

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew. This entry goes with 51:44 and 51:46-49: one block is missing from the Greek.
b: Revelation 18:4 has the same call, 'Come out of her, my people', in Greek.

readings.w: Septuagint (Greek 28:47, Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus)

p: The Greek has no 51:48.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: Then the heavens and the earth / and all that is in them / will shout for joy over Babylon, / for from the north the destroyers will come to her, / the LORD declares.

readings.w: Septuagint (Greek 28:48, Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus)

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew. This entry goes with 51:44-49.
b: The verse is part of the block missing from the Greek, 51:44b-49a.

a: Babylon too must fall, / for the slain of Israel,
t: Babylon must fall for the slain of Israel
p: The Greek has only the second half: 'and in Babylon the wounded of all the earth will fall'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: Babylon too must fall, / for the slain of Israel,

readings.w: Septuagint (Greek 28:49, Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus)

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew. This entry goes with 51:44-48. The Greek's second half agrees with the Hebrew's 'the slain of all the earth'.
b: The Hebrew sentence is hard (see the note). The shorter Greek may reflect an earlier text or an easier one.

a: when he went with Zedekiah king of Judah to Babylon
t: With Zedekiah or from Zedekiah?
p: One letter in Hebrew (m) makes the difference.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: when he went with Zedekiah king of Judah to Babylon

readings.w: Septuagint (Greek 28:59, Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus)
readings.plain: when he went from Zedekiah king of Judah to Babylon

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew. The Hebrew 'et ('with') and me'et ('from') differ by one letter. The Greek's 'from' makes Seraiah an envoy; the Hebrew makes him a member of the king's party.
b: Jeremiah 29:3 mentions an embassy sent by Zedekiah to Babylon in these years, which supports an envoy reading. The Hebrew 'with' fits a trip by the king himself, for which there is no other evidence. Both readings fit the date, the fourth year of Zedekiah (594/593 BC).

a: Seraiah was the officer in charge of rest stops.
t: Rest stops or gifts?
p: One Hebrew word is menuchah 'rest' or minchah 'gift, tribute'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: Seraiah was the officer in charge of rest stops.

readings.w: Septuagint (Greek 28:59, Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus)
readings.plain: Seraiah was the officer in charge of gifts.

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew: 'rest' (menuchah) is the harder word, with a meaning (a quartermaster arranging the king's halting places) that fits a traveling court.
b: The Greek 'chief of gifts' would be a sar minchah, an officer who carried tribute to Babylon, which also fits the trip. Others read 'quartermaster'. The two Hebrew words differ by one letter.

a: and they will wear themselves out.
t: The tired peoples
p: The last clause of Seraiah's words is not in the Greek.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: and they will wear themselves out.

readings.w: Septuagint (Greek 28:64, Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus)

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew but notes that the clause copies the end of 51:58 ('and they wear themselves out'). A copyist may have repeated it here, and the Greek's shorter text points that way.
b: The Greek ends Seraiah's words with 'from the face of the Chaldeans whom I bring on her' where the Hebrew has 'because of the disaster I am bringing on her'. The difference in the closing words is another sign of an earlier form.

a: Up to this point are the words of Jeremiah.
t: The closing note
p: The Greek has no note that Jeremiah's words end here.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: Up to this point are the words of Jeremiah.

readings.w: Septuagint (Greek 28:64, Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus)

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew. Chapter 52 is from 2 Kings, so a note marking the end of Jeremiah's own words is natural in the Hebrew.
b: In the Greek, chapter 52 follows the Babylon oracle with no break. The note is of the same kind as Job 31:40 and Psalm 72:20.

a: He did what was evil in the LORD's eyes, just as Jehoiakim had done.
t: Verse 2 (not in the Greek)
p: The Greek has no verses 2-3.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: He did what was evil in the LORD's eyes, just as Jehoiakim had done.

readings.w: Septuagint (Greek 52:2, Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus)

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew. The same words are in 2 Kings 24:19, so the Hebrew of Jeremiah 52 agrees with the Hebrew of Kings.
b: The Greek goes from the queen mother's name straight to the siege (52:4). The Hebrew of 2 Kings 24:19-20 has these verses.

a: All this happened in Jerusalem and Judah because the LORD was angry, until at last he flung them away from his face. Then Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.
t: Verse 3 (not in the Greek)
p: The Greek has no verses 2-3.

readings.plain: All this happened in Jerusalem and Judah because the LORD was angry, until at last he flung them away from his face. Then Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.

readings.w: Septuagint (Greek 52:3, Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus)

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew; verse 3 is the same as 2 Kings 24:20.
b: This entry goes with verse 2.

a: on the tenth day of the tenth month
t: The tenth month or the ninth?
p: The Greek says ninth month.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: on the tenth day of the tenth month

readings.w: Septuagint (Greek 52:4, Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus)
readings.plain: on the tenth day of the ninth month
readings.orig: ἐν μηνὶ τῷ ἐνάτῳ δεκάτῃ τοῦ μηνός

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew. The tenth month is also in 2 Kings 25:1, Jeremiah 39:1 and Ezekiel 24:1, and Zechariah 8:19 knows a fast of the tenth month. The Greek's 'ninth' is a lone difference.
b: Nothing in the other witnesses supports 'ninth', so it is most likely a slip in the Greek or in its source.

a: On the ninth day of the fourth month,
t: Is 'the fourth month' in the text?
p: The Greek, like the Hebrew of 2 Kings 25:3, has only 'the ninth day of the month'.

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew of Jeremiah, which names the month. Jeremiah 39:2 also says the fourth month, and the site's Plain of 2 Kings supplies it.
b: The Greek and the Hebrew of 2 Kings agree in leaving the month out. The month may have been added in Jeremiah to make the date clear, or dropped in the other two texts. No Qumran copy preserves this verse.

a: He put him in prison until the day he died.
t: Prison, or mill house?
p: The Greek has 'mill house'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: He put him in prison until the day he died.

readings.w: Septuagint (Greek 52:11, Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus)
readings.plain: He put him in the mill house until the day he died.

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew and gives its sense as 'prison'. Beit happequdot is a rare phrase, literally 'house of the appointments' and read as 'of punishments', 'of oversight' or 'of the guards'; 'prison' is the sense all three share.
b: The Greek 'mill house' recalls Samson grinding grain in prison (Judges 16:21). 2 Kings 25:7 has no such line at all.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008)
readings.plain: lifted up the head of Jehoiachin king of Judah and brought him out of the prison house

readings.w: Septuagint (Greek 52:31, Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus)
readings.plain: took the head of Jehoiachin king of Judah, cut his hair, and brought him out of the house where he was kept
readings.orig: ἔλαβεν ... τὴν κεφαλὴν Ἰωακεὶμ ... καὶ ἔκειρεν αὐτόν

why: The Plain follows the Hebrew. 'Lift up the head' is a known idiom for honoring or releasing (Genesis 40:13, 20).
b: The Greek's 'cut his hair' may rest on a different Hebrew reading or on an attempt to make sense of the idiom. 2 Kings 25:27 has the Hebrew idiom as Jeremiah has it.
